items.followUp: State two ways enzymes are used in the textile industry.

rubric.why: Shows one important use of enzymes in paper recycling.
rubric.description: Enzymes help remove ink from recycled paper.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking enzymes with ink removal or deinking in recycled paper.

rubric.why: Shows another industrial use of enzymes in paper manufacture.
rubric.description: Enzymes help in pulp bleaching and can improve paper processing or quality.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid use in pulp bleaching or paper processing.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are used to remove ink from recycled paper during deinking.
They are also used in pulp bleaching and to improve paper processing.

items.followUp: Give two uses of enzymes in the food industry.

rubric.why: Identifies a major cardiovascular effect of saturated fats.
rubric.description: Saturated fatty acids can raise LDL (bad) cholesterol and increase the risk of atherosclerosis or coronary heart disease.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for increased LDL/bad cholesterol or a linked cardiovascular disease.

rubric.why: Recognizes another harmful health effect associated with high saturated-fat intake.
rubric.description: Excess intake can contribute to obesity and related health problems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obesity, weight gain, or another valid health consequence.

modelAnswer: Saturated fatty acids can raise the level of LDL (bad) cholesterol in the blood.
This can lead to atherosclerosis and increase the risk of coronary heart disease; excess intake may also contribute to obesity.

items.followUp: Define an ecosystem and name its two main components.

rubric.why: A population is defined by both species identity and the area in which its members live.
rubric.description: Population level: organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for same species and 1 mark for living in the same area (at the same time).

rubric.why: A community consists of multiple populations of different species living and interacting in an area.
rubric.description: Community level: populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for different species/populations and 1 mark for their shared area or interactions.

modelAnswer: Population level: A population consists of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
Community level: A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and one function of the cell wall.

rubric.why: The membrane’s basic structure is a double layer of phospholipids.
rubric.description: Structure: the cell membrane is a thin, flexible phospholipid bilayer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the bilayer and 1 mark for describing its phospholipid nature.

rubric.why: Membrane proteins are an essential part of the membrane structure.
rubric.description: Proteins are embedded in the bilayer and some form channels or carriers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for embedded proteins or membrane channels/carriers.

rubric.why: Selective permeability is a key membrane function.
rubric.description: The membrane selectively controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for control or regulation of movement across the membrane.

rubric.why: A labeled diagram demonstrates understanding of the membrane’s arrangement.
rubric.description: Diagram: draw a schematic phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins and label the phospholipids, proteins, and outside/inside of the cell; it need not be to scale.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable, appropriately labeled bilayer diagram.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible boundary around the cell, made mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
It is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
Diagram steps: draw two parallel rows of phospholipid heads, with the fatty-acid tails facing inward between the rows.
Add one or more proteins crossing or embedded in the bilayer; label phospholipid heads, fatty-acid tails, protein, outside of cell, and cytoplasm.
Draw the diagram schematically and label it; no scale is specified.

items.followUp: Define a threatened species and give two examples found in Pakistan.

rubric.why: The central feature of an endangered species is its high risk of extinction.
rubric.description: An endangered species is one whose numbers have fallen so greatly that it faces a serious risk of extinction.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for defining the species as being at risk/in danger of extinction, with the severity made clear.

rubric.why: Examples make the definition specific to endangered wildlife in Pakistan.
rubric.description: Examples in Pakistan include the Indus dolphin, snow leopard, markhor, Houbara bustard, and Marco Polo sheep.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each valid Pakistan example, up to 2 marks.

modelAnswer: An endangered species is a species whose population has declined so greatly that it faces a serious risk of extinction.
Examples of endangered species in Pakistan include the Indus dolphin and the snow leopard; the markhor and Houbara bustard are other examples.

items.followUp: What is anaerobic respiration? State where it occurs in a cell.

rubric.why: Defines aerobic respiration by its use of oxygen and release of energy.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for glucose breakdown using oxygen and releasing energy.

rubric.why: Glycolysis is the first stage and produces pyruvate in the cytoplasm.
rubric.description: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into two pyruvic acid molecules, producing a small amount of ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the location and principal product, or an equivalent correct description of glycolysis.

rubric.why: The Krebs cycle oxidizes products of glycolysis and releases carbon dioxide and electron carriers.
rubric.description: The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondria and releases carbon dioxide while transferring energy to electron carriers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct Krebs-cycle account, including location or key products.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor and produces most ATP.
rubric.description: The electron transport chain operates on the inner mitochondrial membrane; oxygen accepts electrons and combines with hydrogen to form water, and most ATP is produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chain’s location/role and 1 mark for oxygen forming water or production of most ATP.

modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: one glucose molecule is split into two pyruvic acid molecules, with a small amount of ATP produced.
The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondria: products derived from pyruvate are oxidized, carbon dioxide is released, and energy is transferred to electron carriers.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane: electrons pass along carriers, oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water, and most ATP is produced.

items.followUp: Explain how excessive pesticide use can harm an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Runoff transfers excess nutrients from fields into waterways.
rubric.description: Rain can wash fertilizers into rivers and lakes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fertilizer runoff into surface water.

rubric.why: Excess nutrients promote eutrophication and algal blooms.
rubric.description: Nutrient enrichment causes excessive algal growth (eutrophication).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for eutrophication or excessive algal growth.

rubric.why: Decomposition of excess algae reduces dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic organisms.
rubric.description: When algae die and decompose, dissolved oxygen falls, which can kill fish and other aquatic organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen depletion or its effect on aquatic life.

rubric.why: Excess fertilizer can also contaminate groundwater or damage soil.
rubric.description: Nitrates may leach into groundwater, and excessive fertilizer use can contribute to soil acidification or salinity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for nitrate contamination or a valid soil-related hazard.

modelAnswer: Rain may wash excess fertilizers from fields into rivers and lakes.
The added nutrients can cause eutrophication and excessive algal growth.
When the algae die, their decomposition uses dissolved oxygen; oxygen depletion can kill fish and other aquatic life.
Nitrates may also leach into groundwater, while excessive fertilizer use can damage soil through acidification or salinity.

items.followUp: Define translocation and name the plant tissue through which it occurs.

rubric.why: Transpiration is defined as water loss from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly leaves.
rubric.description: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, chiefly through the stomata of leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as loss of water vapour from a plant, especially leaves.

rubric.why: Light and warmth generally promote evaporation and stomatal opening, increasing transpiration.
rubric.description: Greater light intensity and higher temperature generally increase the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the effect of light or temperature.

rubric.why: Humidity controls the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and surrounding air.
rubric.description: High humidity decreases transpiration; dry air or low humidity increases it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of humidity.

rubric.why: Air movement removes moist air around leaves and affects the diffusion gradient.
rubric.description: Wind usually increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf; still air reduces it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of wind or air movement.

rubric.why: The plant’s water supply affects stomatal opening and the rate of water loss.
rubric.description: Adequate soil water supports transpiration; water shortage causes stomata to close and reduces the rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the effect of soil-water availability or shortage.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
Light: greater light intensity generally opens stomata and increases transpiration.
Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation and usually increases transpiration.
Humidity: high humidity lowers the water-vapour gradient and decreases transpiration; dry air increases it.
Wind: moving air carries away moist air around the leaf and usually increases transpiration.
Soil water: adequate water supports transpiration, while water shortage causes stomata to close and reduces the rate.
